name: Moringa

lead: Moringa is a tree grown across the tropics. In skin care its seed oil and leaf extracts appear in moisturisers and body oils, marketed for moisturising and antioxidant effects.
Laboratory studies show leaf extracts have antioxidant activity, but no human trial found tests it for skin appearance.

paras: Proposed benefits rest on its fatty-acid-rich oil acting as an emollient and on phenolic compounds such as quercetin and kaempferol that show antioxidant activity in the lab.

Topical products are generally labelled for external use. Oral use has limited human toxicity data and possible drug-metabolism interactions per Wikipedia, and Australia and New Zealand declined novel-food approval in 2025.

lead: Moringa usually refers to Moringa oleifera, a fast-growing tree native to northern India and widely cultivated across the tropics, also known as the drumstick or horseradish tree. Its leaves, pods and seeds are eaten, and its seed oil (sometimes called ben oil) is used as a base in skin- and hair-care products.[1]

In cosmetics, moringa appears as a seed oil or leaf extract in creams, body oils and similar products, typically marketed for moisturising or antioxidant benefits. Laboratory studies have measured antioxidant activity in leaf extracts.[2][3] Published review literature describes the plant mainly in terms of nutrition and general medicinal use rather than controlled evidence for facial appearance.[4][5]

Wikipedia states that despite considerable preliminary research, no high-quality evidence has been found that moringa affects health or disease.[1] No clinical trial found in the registries searched tests moringa for skin appearance.

paras: Moringa oleifera is a tree reaching roughly 10 to 12 metres with feathery leaves and long three-sided pods. Mature seeds yield about 38 to 40 percent oil.[1] Reviews describe the leaves as containing minerals, protein, vitamins, beta-carotene and phenolic compounds such as quercetin and kaempferol.[2][4]

Wikipedia notes that moringa seed oil can serve as a base for cosmetics and for hair and skin care.[1] A US over-the-counter product listing shows moringa seed oil as one ingredient in a topical body oil sold for stretch marks, alongside other plant oils, with labelling for external use only.[6] Such listings describe marketing claims rather than demonstrated effects.

No human studies on moringa for skin appearance were found. Registered human trials have looked at other uses, including leaf extract in rheumatoid arthritis, leaf intake in prediabetes and metabolic syndrome, and moringa toothpastes and varnishes in oral health.[7][8] Safety and efficacy reviews of the plant note that human evidence is limited.[5] Laboratory work has measured the antioxidant capacity of leaf extracts.[3]

Wikipedia reports that human toxicity data are limited, that moringa may interact with cytochrome P450 drug metabolism, and that in November 2025 Food Standards Australia New Zealand rejected an application to approve moringa leaves, pods and oil as a novel food, citing insufficient safety evidence.[1] These points concern ingestion rather than topical cosmetic use.

timeline.event: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck formally describes Moringa oleifera.[1]
